title: Rates of Reaction and Collision Theory
seo_title: Year 11 Chemistry: Rates of Reaction Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_code: Chemistry Unit 2: Rates of chemical reactions
standard_text: Collision theory; the effect of temperature, concentration, surface area and catalysts on reaction rate; Maxwell–Boltzmann energy distributions; energy profile diagrams; measuring and graphing rates of reaction. (Senior Secondary Chemistry, Unit 2: Molecular interactions and reactions)
meta_desc: Free Year 11 Chemistry worksheets on reaction rates: collision theory, temperature, concentration, surface area, catalysts, Maxwell–Boltzmann curves, energy profiles and rate graphs. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Rate depends on how often particles collide with enough energy.
key_sub: A catalyst lowers the activation energy; it is not used up.
body_html:
How to think about it

For a reaction, particles must collide with at least the activation energy and the right orientation. Higher concentration or pressure and larger surface area make collisions more frequent; higher temperature makes collisions more frequent and, more importantly, more energetic.

A Maxwell–Boltzmann curve shows the spread of particle energies; only particles beyond Eₐ can react. A catalyst provides a pathway with a lower Eₐ. Rate is measured from the gradient of a graph of product or reactant against time.

Example

40 mL of gas in the first 20 s. Mean rate?

40 ÷ 20

Answer: 2.0 mL/s

Example

Concentration falls from 0.80 to 0.20 mol/L in 60 s. Mean rate?

(0.80 − 0.20) ÷ 60

Answer: 0.010 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹

Common mistakes

  • Saying a catalyst gives particles more energy.
  • Thinking higher temperature only makes particles collide more often: energy matters most.
  • Drawing the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve with a bigger area at a higher temperature.

faq.q: Why does a small temperature rise make a big difference to rate?
faq.a: It greatly increases the fraction of particles with energy above the activation energy, so many more collisions are successful.
They make reactions faster at lower temperatures, saving energy and money, and they can be reused.

items.q: What happens to the activation energy when a catalyst is added?
c: a different route with a lower activation energy is used
it stays the same but molecules move faster
items.e: The original route is still there; the catalysed route is easier.

items.q: A reaction mixture is at equilibrium. More reactant is added. What happens?
c: the equilibrium shifts to the right
the equilibrium shifts to the left
items.e: The system uses up some of the added reactant.

items.q: What does a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution show?
c: the energy of products and reactants
the number of collisions per second
the number of particles with each kinetic energy at one temperature
items.e: The area under the curve is the total number of particles.

items.q: The acid is diluted with water. What happens to the reaction rate?
items.e: Fewer particles per volume means fewer collisions.

items.q: Why are enzymes important industrial catalysts?
c: they work only at high temperature
they work at low temperatures and are very specific, saving energy
items.e: Enzymes are used in detergents and food processing.

items.q: A catalyst is added to CO + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub> (the water–gas shift reaction) at equilibrium. What happens?

items.q: What happens to the rate of a gas reaction if the pressure is doubled?
c: it increases, because the particles are closer together
items.e: Higher pressure means higher concentration of gas.

items.q: Why does increasing concentration increase the rate of reaction?
c: there are more particles in the same volume, so collisions are more frequent

items.q: Why does powdered marble react faster with acid than marble chips?
c: the powder has a larger surface area, so more collisions happen

items.q: The gas is squeezed into a smaller container. Which explains the change in rate?
c: Higher pressure packs gas particles closer, so they collide more often.
Lower temperature and no light slow its decomposition.
A catalyst gives a path with lower activation energy.

items.q: What is Le Chatelier's principle?
c: pressure has no effect on gases
equilibrium always lies to the right
a system at equilibrium shifts to oppose a change in conditions
items.e: Use it to predict the effect of changing temperature, pressure or concentration.

items.q: A catalyst is added to CH<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ CO + 3H<sub>2</sub> (steam reforming) at equilibrium. What happens?
c: the equilibrium shifts to the right
the equilibrium shifts to the left

items.e: A catalyst speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally.

items.q: On a graph of volume of gas against time, what does a steeper slope mean?
c: less gas is made in total

items.q: Which change would NOT increase the rate of reaction between zinc and hydrochloric acid?
items.e: Larger lumps have less surface area.

items.q: Which part of the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve shows the molecules that can react?
c: the area to the right of the activation energy
the area to the left of the activation energy
the point where the curve starts
items.e: Only these molecules have enough energy.

items.q: What is the activation energy?
c: the average kinetic energy of the molecules
the minimum energy needed for a reaction to happen
the energy released by a reaction
items.e: Collisions with less energy do not react.

items.q: Why does the rate of reaction decrease as the reaction goes on?
c: reactants are used up, so their concentration falls
items.e: The curve levels off when a reactant runs out.

items.q: How does a catalyst increase the rate of reaction?
c: it gives particles more kinetic energy
it provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy
it is used up in the reaction
items.e: The catalyst is unchanged at the end.

items.q: Why are catalytic converters fitted to car exhausts?
c: they speed up the conversion of CO, NO and unburnt fuel into less harmful gases
items.e: They contain platinum, palladium and rhodium.

items.q: What happens to the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve at a higher temperature?
c: the peak moves to the right and gets lower
the peak moves to the left and gets higher
the curve starts at a higher energy
the area under the curve increases
items.e: More molecules have higher energies, but the total number is the same.

items.q: The acid is heated from 20 °C to 40 °C. What happens to the reaction rate?
items.e: Particles move faster, so they collide more often and more collisions have enough energy.

items.q: On a Maxwell–Boltzmann diagram, how does a catalyst change the picture?
c: the activation energy line moves to the left, so more particles have enough energy
items.e: The distribution itself does not change.

items.q: How can the rate of the reaction between magnesium and acid be measured?
c: measure the colour of the acid

items.e: A gas syringe collects the gas.

items.q: A catalyst is added. What happens to the reaction rate?

items.q: According to collision theory, what must happen for particles to react?

items.q: What does 'dynamic equilibrium' mean?
